[The reframe]{.kicker}

## The spreadsheet is the comparison layer

This is not remedial Excel. A workbook is the most portable way to make a **generative comparison of variants** legible to someone else.

::: {.concept-card}
[Why it earns its place]{.card-title}
It is the lowest-friction surface where assumptions, options, and trade-offs sit side by side and stay editable.
:::

- visible assumptions, not hidden ones
- editable comparison logic anyone can rerun
- traceable calculations from input to claim
- fast iteration with no heavy setup

---

## Where it sits on the spine

::: {.spine-rail}
[Decision]{.node} [Evidence]{.node} [Variation]{.node .is-current} [Output]{.node} [Threshold]{.node} [Action]{.node}
:::

The workbook is how **Variation** becomes inspectable: many variants or scenarios, one comparable structure, one readable output.

::: {.warning-card}
A1 is **finalized** this week — the Total Recall board. The comparison habit you build here is exactly what A2's Workflow Map will formalize.
:::

[Tool demo]{.kicker}

## Workbook anatomy

The same four-zone frame we use for every tool. This is a minimum runnable workbook, not an abstract exercise.

::: {.tool-panel}
::: {.zone .input}
**Input** `variant`, `criterion`, `value`, `unit`, `source`, `confidence`
:::
::: {.zone .operation}
**What varies** weights, thresholds, variant rows, confidence notes
:::
::: {.zone .output}
**Output** live workbook, decision table, chart, `variant_scores.csv`
:::
::: {.zone .check}
**Quality check** formulas visible, units stated, one hand calculation matches
:::
:::

## Start with the decision, not the software

The structure follows the question, never the other way around.

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.warning-card}
[Workbook with no decision]{.card-title}

- one giant undifferentiated sheet
- no units, no audience
- columns with no reason to exist
:::

::: {.activity-card}
[Workbook built on a decision]{.card-title}

- one question per structure
- one row type per sheet
- one clear output already in mind
:::
::::

---

## A useful workbook pattern

Three sheets, each tied to one job in the comparison.

:::: {.three-step}
::: {.step-box}
[Sheet 1 · Evidence log]{.card-title}
source · date · evidence type · relevance · confidence
:::
::: {.step-box}
[Sheet 2 · Alternatives]{.card-title}
option · criteria · scores or ranges · comments
:::
::: {.step-box}
[Sheet 3 · Outputs]{.card-title}
the chart · the matrix · the summary line
:::
::::

::: {.concept-card}
Each sheet answers one question, so the reader never has to reverse-engineer your intent.
:::

## From image to comparable fields

![High Line, New York](../assets/examples/high-line-park.jpg){height="380"}

If you claimed this public-space strategy works, what would the workbook need to **compare**? Move from atmosphere to comparable fields: location, activity type, time and duration, seating/circulation, weather, evidence source and confidence.

---

## Typical comparison uses

- precedent comparison across variants
- evidence and source logging
- option scoring with stated criteria
- uncertainty-range charts
- summary tables for a decision brief

::: {.reflection-card}
Every one of these is a way of laying variants side by side so the trade-off becomes visible to someone who was not in your head.
:::

---

[The chart problem]{.kicker}

## Bad chart vs cleaned chart

A chart fails when it describes data instead of carrying a message.

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.warning-card}
[The chart that fails a stakeholder]{.card-title}

- too many series, no dominant takeaway
- labels too small to read at a glance
- colour decorating instead of working
- title naming the data, not the message
:::

::: {.activity-card}
[The cleaned chart]{.card-title}

- one message, stated in the title
- only the series that support it
- annotation forcing the eye to the point
- uncertainty shown where it matters
:::
::::

---

## The 3-second message test

If a critic glances for three seconds, can they tell:

- what is being compared?
- which option is stronger or riskier?
- what they are meant to notice?

::: {.warning-card}
If not, the chart is not finished — that is a clarity gap, not a failure of taste.
:::

---

## Chart rescue formula

::: {.recall-4step}
::: {.step}
**Message** Decide the one thing the chart must say
:::
::: {.step}
**Remove** Cut everything that does not support it
:::
::: {.step}
**Force** Use annotation or labels to make the point unmissable
:::
::: {.step}
**Limit** Show uncertainty, then connect back to the decision
:::
:::

---

## Show uncertainty honestly

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.warning-card}
[Avoid]{.card-title}

- fake precision
- unexplained weighted scores
- single-point claims on weak inputs
:::

::: {.activity-card}
[Prefer]{.card-title}

- ranges and scenario labels
- note fields for assumptions
- charts that make limits visible
:::
::::

---

## Decision matrix example

A matrix is a comparison layer in table form — readable as long as the criteria and direction are stated.

| Option | daylight | access | cost | risk | recommendation note |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| A | high | medium | medium | medium | balanced |
| B | medium | high | low | high | cheaper but riskier |
| C | high | high | high | low | strongest, but costly |

::: {.reflection-card}
The note column is doing the real work: it converts scores back into a defensible recommendation.
:::

---

[Uncertainty check]{.kicker}

## A number is not neutral just because it is in a cell

::: {.uncertainty-check}
**Question for your workbook**
Which cell, weight, or threshold would change the recommendation if it moved by 10 percent?
:::

That cell is not a detail. It is a design assumption wearing the costume of arithmetic.

---

[ML principle connection]{.kicker}

## When you weight a decision matrix, you are writing a loss function

::: {.concept-card}
[Principle 4 — Loss = what "better" means]{.card-title}
An ML model only improves on what its loss rewards. Your spreadsheet's weights are the same thing: they define what "better" means before you compare anything.
:::

::: {.reflection-card}
[So]{.card-title}
If your weighting ignores a real constraint (cost, daylight, legibility), the "winning" variant will too. Make the criterion explicit, like a loss.
:::

See [ML Primer · Principles 3–4](../lectures/ml-primer-12-principles.html).

---

[Anecdote · when the spreadsheet hides the risk]{.kicker}

## 2012: a copy-paste error inside a risk model

::: {.warning-card}
[What happened]{.card-title}
JPMorgan's "London Whale" risk model lived in a chain of spreadsheets where values were **copied and pasted between cells by hand**. One step divided by a sum instead of an average, understating the risk. The losses reached about US$6 billion.
:::

::: {.example-card}
[The lesson]{.card-title}
A spreadsheet is a transparent comparison layer only if its steps are inspectable. Manual copy-paste between cells is exactly where the logic stops being traceable.
:::

## Mode 1 — the walk-through (optional, celebrated)

This is a hands-on tool week, so a live walk-through is especially welcome.

::: {.walkthrough-card}
[Show us your workbook running]{.card-title}
A volunteer opens their actual spreadsheet and walks the class through one comparison — uninterrupted, 3–4 minutes. Messy is fine; we want the real thing working.
:::

- not graded as a performance; volunteering earns credit, never penalty
- the room listens; questions wait for the audit
- show how a variant changes the output live, if you can

---

## Reconstruct your comparison in four steps

**Object this week: your comparison of variants or scenarios in a spreadsheet.**

::: {.recall-4step}
::: {.step}
**Did** What variants did I compare, and how did I structure the sheets?
:::
::: {.step}
**Assumed** What scores, weights, or units did I treat as given?
:::
::: {.step}
**Risk** Where is the comparison hiding a weak input or a false precision?
:::
::: {.step}
**Verify** What would I add to make the trade-off legible to a stranger?
:::
:::

::: {.grading-note}
Post your filled four-step to Slack under your comparison. Posting + an honest reconstruction is the graded unit — not how you spoke or how polished the workbook looks.
:::

Volunteers go first; random draw may fill the remaining examples.

---

## Peer-swap test

Swap screens with a classmate. They read only what is on the sheet — you stay quiet.

::: {.audit-card}
[Examine the workbook, not the author]{.card-title}
Can a reader, with no narration:

- follow the workbook logic quickly?
- tell what each column means?
- identify the decision being supported?
- read the chart without explanation?
:::

Where the answer is no, that is a fix on the artifact — not a judgment of the person.

---

## What the spreadsheet cannot replace

- spatial reasoning at city or site scale
- repeated geospatial operations
- heavier notebook automation
- simulation-specific modeling

::: {.concept-card}
That is exactly why the course goes on to survey GIS, BIM/BEM, Grasshopper, Python, and AI-assisted workflows.
:::

---

## If you stay on the spreadsheet

You can do the course very well on this tool, as long as you:

- keep the comparison logic clean
- tie every sheet to a decision
- avoid decorative graphics
- document what the workbook cannot tell you
